newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: WTO may yield pacts on technology, but not labour.
newsitem.headline: WTO may yield pacts on technology, but not labour.

text.p: Big powers at the World Trade Organisation's first Ministerial Conference on Tuesday looked to lucrative accords on booming technologies to provide the silver lining for the storm-clouded global gathering.

The United States served notice it would still push hard to get the explosive issue of labour rights on to the WTO agenda as North and South battled behind the scenes over corruption in trade, investment rules and competition policy.

"There is no question that what the industrialised countries now hope for most here is a deal on information technology products and agreement to work hard for a basic telecommucations pact by February," said one key negotiator. The two chief figures in the infotech debate -- U.S. Acting Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky and European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan -- met over breakfast to try to smooth out differences on what a pact should cover.

The potential accord, known as ITA, would incorporate Asian developing economies playing a growing role in trade in computers and microchips and would remove all tariffs in a sector valued at $600 billion a year by the turn of the century.
Signals from negotiators left little doubt the major traders were aiming for agreement this week -- perhaps by Wednesday.

Japan's Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda told the second day of the Conference he hoped "ardently....that we will have an agreement as the most significant achievement of this ministerial conference in the area of trade liberalisation."

The 128 full delegations from WTO member countries and ministers and officials from nearly 30 others waiting to be admitted to the organisation have also heard ringing appeals for progress to a telecoms liberalisation pact.

Negotiators at WTO headquarters in Geneva are facing a deadline to finalise a deal among some 50 countries by mid-February after failing in an earlier bid last April when the United States pulled out of the talks.

This sector, heavily protected in many emerging economies, is estimated to be worth well over $500 billion annually. Conference host state Singapore is expected to join several others in making new offers this week.
Barshefsky struck a positive note after a U.S-called meeting of telecom negotiators on Monday.

"There was no high drama but it was an important additional step as we move towards February 15," Barshefsky said. Brittan told reporters he hoped new offers, mainly from Asian countries, would help break the back of the negotiations.

As the full Conference resumed on Tuesday, key ministers and their aides from different areas of the globe met in conclave to try to hammer out the final text of a declaration to be issued at the end of the gathering on Friday.

Sixteen of 20 paragraphs have been agreed, but there was no doubt a major battle was under way over the last four -- touching mainly on the "new issues" that have proven the most divisive in Singapore.

Officials said negotiating on whether the declaration, meant to point the WTO down the free trade path into the 21st century, should include any reference at all to the labour issue was being left to last.

Several key emerging economies in Asia -- including India, Malaysia and Indonesia -- are insisting there should be no mention at all, arguing that even a neutral phrasing would suggest work conditions were a subject for the WTO.

Pressured by U.S. and international labour unions, Washington wants the trade watchdog to take the question on board. It is backed by France and Norway, but has run up against opposition from some EU countries as well as from the Asians.

Another contentious issue cutting across North-South lines is agriculture. Members of the Cairns Group of farm produce exporters -- who range from Argentina and Australia to Thailand and Uruguay -- want to move quickly to open markets wider.

They seek a reference in the declaration to preparations for new WTO farm talks set for the end of the century. But they are opposed by the EU, Japan and South Korea, whose farmers are unhappy over deals finalised in the 1994 world trade pact.
